formulas.name: Local solar time of an overpass
formulas.status_text: Running in the pipeline: every detection carries an lmst value and a local_date
formulas.lead: FIRMS stamps every fire pixel with the time in UTC. Fires, farmers and satellites follow the Sun, not Greenwich. This formula moves each detection onto the Sun's clock at the place where it was seen, so that a 13:30 pass means the same thing over Punjab, California and Córdoba.
formulas.reads: Local mean solar time equals the UTC time plus one hour for every 15 degrees of longitude east, wrapped onto a 24-hour clock; the local day is the date on that clock.

symbols.meaning: Acquisition time of the scan, from the FIRMS column acq_time (HHMM)
Longitude of the pixel centre, east positive
Earth turns 360° in 24 h, so the Sun moves 15° of longitude per hour
Local mean solar time of the detection
Local solar day used for every daily count

origin: The relation is as old as navigation. The Earth turns through 360° of longitude in 24 hours, so local noon arrives four minutes later for every degree you travel west. A clock that reads 12:00 when the mean Sun crosses the local meridian is the local mean solar time; the true (apparent) Sun runs up to about 16 minutes ahead of or behind it during the year, a difference called the equation of time, $E(d)$.

FIRMS documents acq_time as the UTC time of the satellite overpass. Polar orbiters such as Terra, Aqua, Suomi NPP and NOAA-20 are designed to cross each latitude at a fixed local solar time, which is why the conversion is the natural clock for them.
why: Three parts of FIREWORK depend on it. First, a fire cell-day (F05) must be a local day. A fire seen at 20:30 UTC over Punjab is already the next morning there; binning by UTC date would put it on the wrong day and, at month ends, in the wrong month of the calendar.

Second, MODIS and VIIRS are compared by overpass. Terra looks in the late morning, Aqua and the VIIRS satellites in the early afternoon. Only on the solar clock do these windows line up the same way everywhere on Earth, so day and night strata (F13) and matched pairs (F20) can be built consistently.

Third, the Blind Spot page asks what share of a day's burning falls inside the moments the satellites look (F45). That question only makes sense on the Sun's clock, because burning follows sunshine and field work, not UTC.
Indian Standard Time is not a substitute. IST is pinned to 82.5°E, so over Punjab (about 74–77°E) it runs about 20–35 minutes ahead of the Sun. Using IST would shift every overpass by that amount.
how: The formula is a shift and a wrap. Converting acq_time 0748 to decimal hours gives $7 + 48/60 = 7.80$ h. Adding $\lambda/15$ moves the clock east or west. The modulo keeps the result between 0 and 24, so a detection at 23:00 UTC at 30°E becomes 01:00 the next local day.
The local date is computed from the same shifted timestamp, not from the UTC date, so every daily and monthly aggregation downstream uses the day that a farmer at that spot would recognise.

Apparent solar time would add $E(d)/60$ hours. FIREWORK bins detections into days and half-hour windows, where the 16-minute equation of time does not change any assignment except right at midnight, so the mean solar time is used and the apparent correction is documented, not applied.
example: A real Aqua detection from the archive: latitude 30.009°N, longitude 75.741°E, acq_time 0748 UTC on 2 November 2023. The longitude offset is 75.74/15 = 5.05 h, so the fire was seen at 12.85 h, or about 12:51 local mean solar time. In IST the same moment reads 13:18, about half an hour ahead of the Sun.

Across all 2.43 million detections in the region, daytime passes cluster tightly: the median daytime local solar time is Terra 10:51, Aqua 13:18, S-NPP 13:10, NOAA-20 13:09. Figure 1 shows how narrow these windows are.

def lmst(utc_hhmm: int, lon: float) -> float:
    """t_LMST = (t_UTC + lon/15) mod 24, in hours."""
    utc_h = utc_hhmm // 100 + (utc_hhmm % 100) / 60
    return (utc_h + lon / 15.0) % 24.0

formulas.name: Pixel footprint and scan-angle growth
formulas.status_text: Uses the scan and track columns delivered by FIRMS; shown on Sensor Lab and the Learn pages
formulas.lead: A fire pixel near the edge of a satellite swath covers far more ground than one straight below the satellite. This formula gives the real ground area each detection stands for, which explains why MODIS and VIIRS dots look so different and why one bigger pixel is not one bigger fire.
formulas.reads: The footprint of a detection is its along-scan size times its along-track size, both supplied by FIRMS; the cosine terms explain why both grow toward the swath edge.

symbols.meaning: Pixel size across the swath (along the scan line)
Pixel size along the satellite's path
View (scan) angle away from straight down
Pixel size at nadir: 1 km for MODIS, 375 m for VIIRS I-band
Ground footprint of one detection

origin: A scanning radiometer looks sideways through a rotating mirror. As the view angle θ grows, the line of sight gets longer and meets the ground at a slant. On a flat Earth the across-scan size grows as $1/\cos^2\theta$ and the along-track size as $1/\cos\theta$. On the real, curved Earth the growth is stronger: a 1 km MODIS pixel becomes about 4.8 km by 2.0 km at the 55° swath edge.

Rather than recomputing this geometry, FIRMS publishes the actual dimensions of every pixel in the columns scan and track, derived from the instrument geolocation. Multiplying them gives the footprint. VIIRS limits its own growth by aggregating detector samples near nadir and deleting overlapping 'bow-tie' samples, so its pixels grow far less.
why: FIREWORK compares counts from two sensors whose pixels differ by a factor of about six in area at nadir and by much more at the swath edge. Without this formula it is tempting to read the large MODIS squares on a map as large fires. They are not: the footprint is the size of the observation, not the size of the fire inside it.

The footprint also explains the exchange rate k (F11–F14). A small field fire covers a tiny share of a 1–10 km² MODIS pixel and may not raise its temperature enough to trigger detection, while it can fill a meaningful share of a 0.14 km² VIIRS pixel. That geometry is a main reason VIIRS reports more fire cell-days than MODIS for the same farms.
Footprints are also the basis for sensitivity checks, for example repeating a calculation using only near-nadir MODIS pixels, and for the 'why the dots differ' explanation on Sensor Lab.
how: For every detection the pipeline keeps scan and track exactly as FIRMS delivers them. The footprint is their product. No angle is needed because FIRMS has already solved the geometry, including Earth curvature.

The cosine law is kept as intuition only. Starting from nadir, the slant distance to the ground is $h/\cos\theta$ for orbit height $h$, which stretches the pixel by $1/\cos\theta$ along track; across the scan the ground is also tilted relative to the line of sight, adding another $1/\cos\theta$. On a sphere, the local incidence angle exceeds θ, so the true growth is larger than this sketch.
example: In the Punjab + Haryana archive the median MODIS footprint is 1.21 km² and 95% of MODIS detections are smaller than 3.90 km²; the largest edge pixels reach 4.8 km × 2.0 km = 9.6 km². For VIIRS the median is 0.20 km² and the maximum 0.62 km². About 20% of MODIS detections represent more than 2 km² of ground.

formulas.name: Grid cell index
formulas.status_text: Running in the pipeline: every detection is assigned a 0.1° cell_id
formulas.lead: Points from two sensors never fall on the same coordinates. To compare them, FIREWORK drops every detection into a fixed 0.1° grid that is the same for every sensor, every year and every region. This formula turns a latitude and longitude into that grid cell, robustly, even at exact cell edges.
formulas.reads: Shift latitude and longitude so they start at zero, divide by the cell size, round to nine decimals to remove floating-point noise, take the whole number, and keep it inside the grid.

symbols.meaning: Latitude and longitude of the detection
Cell size, 0.1°
Round to 9 decimal places before the floor
Maps longitude into [−180, 180)
Row (0–1799) and column (0–3599)
One integer per cell, row × 3600 + column

origin: A regular latitude–longitude grid is the simplest common frame for gridded Earth data; the 0.1° size is a FIREWORK analysis choice, close to the VIIRS 375 m to MODIS 1 km scale range and small enough to separate villages and districts. NASA does not provide this grid.

The floor of a scaled coordinate is the textbook way to bin. The rounding step comes from computing practice: decimal numbers such as 28.1 cannot be stored exactly in binary, so $(28.1+90)/0.1$ evaluates to 1180.9999999999998 and a plain floor sends a point sitting exactly on a cell edge into the cell below.
why: Every count on the site starts here. The fire cell-day (F05), the monthly count (F06), the cell areas (F04) and the region membership table all use the same cell_id. If two sensors used two grids, or if edge points flipped between cells, the comparison between MODIS and VIIRS would carry an artificial difference that no calibration could remove.
The grid is also what lets FIREWORK be global: one index scheme covers the Earth, and a region is simply a list of cell ids with the fraction of each cell inside its boundary.
how: • Wrap longitude into [−180, 180).• Shift: $\varphi+90$ runs 0–180 and $\lambda+180$ runs 0–360.• Divide by Δ = 0.1 to count cells from the south-west corner of the world.• Round to 9 decimals so values like 1180.9999999999998 become 1181 before the floor.• Floor, then clamp: latitude 90 or longitude 180 would create a row or column outside the grid, so they are held to the last one.• Combine row and column into one integer.
example: A fire near Ludhiana at 30.91°N, 75.85°E: $i = \lfloor (30.91+90)/0.1 \rfloor = 1209$ and $j = \lfloor (75.85+180)/0.1 \rfloor = 2558$, so cell_id = 1209 × 3600 + 2558 = 4354958. That cell spans 30.9–31.0°N and 75.8–75.9°E.

The rounding step is not cosmetic. Testing every exact 0.1° cell edge on Earth, a plain floor sends 643 of the 1,800 latitude edges and 1287 of the 3,600 longitude edges into the wrong cell. With rounding to nine decimals the count is 0. FIRMS coordinates are stored with up to five decimals, so real detections do land on exact edges.

formulas.code:
import math
def cell_index(lat: float, lon: float, d: float = 0.1) -> int:
    """i = floor(round9((lat+90)/d)), j = floor(round9((wrap(lon)+180)/d)), clamped."""
    lon = ((lon + 180) % 360) - 180
    i = min(math.floor(round((lat + 90) / d, 9)), int(180 / d) - 1)
    j = min(math.floor(round((lon + 180) / d, 9)), int(360 / d) - 1)
    return i * int(360 / d) + j

formulas.name: Area of a grid cell on the sphere
formulas.status_text: Running in the pipeline: area_km2 stored for every cell and cell-month
formulas.lead: A 0.1° cell is not a fixed number of square kilometres: it is 124 km² at the equator and 106 km² over Punjab. This formula gives the exact area of a latitude–longitude cell on a spherical Earth, so densities and regional totals compare fairly between latitudes.
formulas.reads: The area of a cell is the Earth's radius squared, times the cell's width in radians, times the difference of the sines of its north and south edges; a region adds up the share of each cell that lies inside it.

symbols.meaning: Mean Earth radius (IUGG)
Cell width, 0.1° expressed in radians
South and north edges of the cell
Share of cell g inside the region polygon
Area of cell g

origin: The formula integrates the area element of a sphere, $dA = R^2\cos\varphi\, d\varphi\, d\lambda$. Integrating $\cos\varphi$ from $\varphi_1$ to $\varphi_2$ gives $\sin\varphi_2-\sin\varphi_1$, and integrating over longitude gives $\Delta\lambda$. The result is exact for a sphere; the WGS84 ellipsoid differs by less than 0.5% at this scale.
R = 6371.0088 km is the IUGG mean radius, the same value used by the haversine distance (F40), so areas and distances in FIREWORK are mutually consistent.
why: Counts per cell mean different things at different latitudes. A cell over Córdoba (about 31–35°S) and one over Punjab hold roughly the same area, but cells over northern Canada are half as large. Any map coloured by 'fires per km²', and any region total built from cell fractions, needs the true area.
Region areas are also a quality check on the region membership table: if the cells and fractions add up to the published area of a state, the polygon overlay is right.
how: The width of a cell shrinks with $\cos\varphi$ toward the poles while its height in kilometres stays the same, so the area falls smoothly from the equator to zero at the poles. Using the sines of the two edges, instead of the cosine at the centre times the height, gives the exact value even for the tiny cells next to the poles.
A region is a set of cells with fractions $f_g$ from intersecting the Natural Earth admin-1 polygon with the grid. Multiplying each cell's area by its fraction and summing gives the region area.
example: A cell from 30.9° to 31.0°N: $A = 6371.0088^2 \times 0.0017453 \times (\sin 31.0^\circ - \sin 30.9^\circ) = 106.0$ km². At the equator the same cell is 123.6 km², at 60°N 61.7 km², and next to the pole 0.108 km². Across Punjab + Haryana cells range from 104.2 km² in the north to 109.5 km² in the south.

Summing all 6,480,000 cells gives 510,065,881 km², equal to $4\pi R^2$ = 510,065,881 km² to the last digit shown. Gridded region areas from cell fractions are Punjab 50,444 km² and Haryana 43,997 km², against published areas of about 50,362 and 44,212 km².

formulas.name: Fire cell-day indicator
formulas.status_text: Running in the pipeline: the cell_day table holds one row per cell, local day, platform and day/night
formulas.lead: VIIRS draws many small dots over a burning village; MODIS draws a few big ones. Counting dots would compare pixel sizes, not fires. The fire cell-day asks one fair question of both sensors: was any fire detected in this 0.1° cell on this local day?
formulas.reads: The cell-day flag is one when platform s detected at least one quality-filtered fire in cell g on local day d during pass δ, and zero otherwise.

symbols.meaning: Number of filtered detections (F07, static sources removed)
Platform: Terra, Aqua, S-NPP, NOAA-20, NOAA-21
0.1° grid cell
Local solar day
Day (D) or night (N) pass
Indicator: 1 if true, 0 if false

origin: Turning point counts into presence–absence per space–time unit is standard in fire climatology. Giglio's MODIS fire climatologies count 'fire pixels' per cell, while studies that compare instruments with different pixel sizes, such as MODIS and VIIRS, use presence per cell and day to remove the pixel-size effect.
The idea is the same as counting 'rainy days' rather than raindrops: it measures how often burning was seen, not how many pixels the burning lit up.
why: The MODIS–VIIRS harmonisation is a comparison of two rulers. If the ruler were 'number of pixels', VIIRS with pixels about six times smaller would read several times higher for the same fire, and the ratio would mostly measure pixel size. With cell-days, both sensors answer a yes/no question about the same 100 km² box on the same day, so the remaining difference is mainly what each sensor can detect (F20), which is exactly what the exchange rate k should capture.

Keeping the platform and the day/night pass in the key matters. It lets FIREWORK fit separate day and night exchange rates (F13), match platforms with similar overpass times (Aqua with S-NPP), and later divide by the number of valid looks of the same platform (F09).
how: Detections that pass the quality rule (F07) and are not static industrial sources are grouped by cell, local day, platform and pass. Any group with at least one detection becomes a cell-day with value 1. Several revisits in a day by the same platform are merged on purpose; they are one opportunity on one day, not several fires.
Alongside the flag, the table keeps how many detections formed it and the maximum and summed fire radiative power, so nothing is lost for later analysis.
example: On 5 November 2023, cell 4322556 near Ludhiana held 37 S-NPP detections, 44 NOAA-20 detections and 9 Aqua detections, all daytime. Each platform contributes exactly one cell-day: $c = 1$ for S-NPP, NOAA-20 and Aqua.

Across the archive (since S-NPP began), an S-NPP cell-day contains 3.7 detections on average and 58% of S-NPP cell-days hold more than one; for MODIS the mean is 2.0. The busiest S-NPP cell-day (2016-11-07, cell 4322555) collapsed 84 detections into one flag. The table has 697,731 rows.

origin: A double sum is the plain way to aggregate a space–time indicator to a region and month. The rule that a missing month is NULL comes from the FIREWORK truth policy: absence of data is not evidence of absence of fire.
why: This is the raw material of everything on the Calendar page and of the calibration. The exchange rate k compares MODIS and VIIRS values of $C$ month by month; the harmonised calendar multiplies MODIS values of $C$ by k; the anomaly z compares this month's $C$ with other years.

The NULL rule is essential. Before S-NPP's archive starts (January 2012) there is no VIIRS value; a month whose download was cut short has an unknown value. Writing zero in either case would create false quiet months and would bias k toward MODIS.
how: The pipeline sums cell-days over cells in the region and days in the month for each sensor family. Separately it records, from the download manifest, how many days of the month were actually fetched for that family. A month with every day covered gets status ok and its count, even if that count is 0. A month with some days missing gets partial and is treated as unknown in calibration; a month never fetched gets not_downloaded and NULL.

formulas.name: Confidence filter (sensor-native)
formulas.status_text: Running in the pipeline: MODIS confidence ≥ 30 and VIIRS nominal or high are counted
formulas.lead: Each sensor grades its own detections, but in different languages: MODIS gives a number from 0 to 100, VIIRS gives a class, low, nominal or high. This formula keeps each sensor in its own language, applies one documented rule per sensor, and measures how much the answer depends on that choice.
formulas.reads: A detection is kept when its own confidence label is in the accepted set for its sensor; the exchange rate is then recomputed under twelve pairs of rules to show how much the rule matters.

symbols.meaning: MODIS detection confidence (FIRMS describes it as experimental)
VIIRS confidence class: low, nominal, high
Accepted set of labels for sensor s
Exchange rate computed after filtering with a rule pair

origin: Both confidence fields are produced inside the NASA detection algorithms. MODIS confidence is a number combining several test scores; VIIRS assigns low confidence mostly to night detections in South Atlantic Anomaly regions and to pixels affected by sun glint, nominal to clear detections, and high to saturated pixels. FIRMS documents both and recommends treating MODIS confidence as experimental.

Neither scale is a calibrated probability. A MODIS 60 is not '60% sure', and there is no published conversion between the MODIS number and the VIIRS class. Mapping classes to numbers such as 0.25/0.6/0.9 would invent precision that does not exist.
why: The exchange rate k is a ratio of two filtered counts. If the filter for one sensor is much stricter than the other, k changes even though the fires did not. FIREWORK therefore fixes one default rule per sensor in its own language and publishes how k moves under other reasonable rules. That spread is part of the honest uncertainty of the harmonised record.
It also keeps the user interface truthful: the confidence control on Explorer is a named rule, not a slider that pretends both sensors share one probability scale.
how: The default keeps MODIS detections with confidence at least 30 and VIIRS detections of class nominal or high. The 30 threshold removes the lowest-scored MODIS pixels while keeping almost all real agricultural fires; nominal + high is FIRMS's own recommended VIIRS default.

For the sensitivity grid the pipeline recomputes Oct–Nov cell-days for both sensors under four MODIS thresholds and three VIIRS class sets and divides them. The default pair sits inside the grid, so a reader can see whether it is typical.
example: In Punjab + Haryana the default rule keeps 97.0% of MODIS vegetation-fire detections and 87.7% of S-NPP detections (classes: nominal 84%, low 12%, high 4%).

For October–November cell-days, 2012–2025, the default rule gives k = 2.27. The eight rule pairs that keep nominal-class VIIRS and MODIS thresholds up to 50 give k between 2.24 and 2.50. Extreme rules move k far: MODIS ≥ 80 raises it to 11.6, and keeping only VIIRS 'high' drops it to 0.19, because high marks saturated pixels, not certain fires.

formulas.name: Persistence (static-source mask)
formulas.status_text: FIRMS static-source flags are removed in the live pipeline; the persistence score is in the reference library and the Sources page
formulas.lead: A brick kiln, a gas flare or a steel plant is hot almost every day of the year. A rice field burns once. Persistence measures how often a site is seen hot out of the days it could have been seen, so steady industrial heat does not inflate the farm-fire calendar or the calibration.
formulas.reads: The persistence of a site is the number of days it was seen hot divided by the number of days it could be observed; with no observable days it is unknown.

symbols.meaning: A site: a grid cell or a cluster of repeated detections (F41)
Hot that day (any filtered detection)
The site was observable that day (clear view)
Share of observable days that were hot

origin: The idea is a frequency of occurrence, widely used to separate persistent thermal anomalies from transient fires. FIRMS itself flags detections of known static sources (the type field: 2 = other static land source, 3 = offshore), and global studies of industrial heat sources (for example gas flares) use multi-year detection frequency in the same way.
why: FIREWORK's calendar and its exchange rate are about vegetation and crop fires. A kiln that is detected on hundreds of days would add the same cell-days every month, raise quiet months and change k in ways that have nothing to do with agriculture. The live pipeline already drops detections FIRMS marks as volcanoes or static sources; persistence extends that to sites FIRMS has not catalogued.
On the Sources page, persistence is one of the pieces of evidence for calling a site agricultural, industrial or uncertain, together with night share (F44) and context (F42–F43).
how: The numerator counts days the site was hot. The denominator counts days the site could have been seen, which comes from the daily fire-mask products (MOD14A1, MYD14A1, VNP14A1) via Earth Engine: a day counts when the pixel is classified as clear land, water or fire, and not when it is cloud or unknown. Dividing by calendar days instead would make cloudy places look less persistent.
When nothing was observable the score is unknown, not zero. A threshold (for example 0.20) to call a site persistent is a hypothesis to be fitted on labelled sites, not a constant.
example: Grouping S-NPP detections into sites of about 400 m, the 51 sites FIRMS marks as static sources were hot on a median of 49 days between 2012 and 2026, and the busiest on 867 days. The 346,905 farm-fire sites were hot on a median of 3 days; only 0.007% of them reached 20 days, against 80% of static sites.

Clear-day counts are not yet loaded for this region, so the exact score is pending. Because observable days cannot exceed calendar days (5,400 since S-NPP began), the busiest static site has $p \ge 867/5400 = 0.16$ even before clouds are taken into account. An illustrative kiln hot on 300 of 365 observable days has $p = 0.82$; a paddy field hot on 7 of 365 has $p = 0.02$.

formulas.name: Clear-sky (exposure) fire rate
formulas.status_text: Defined and wired into the Calendar ('exposure rate'); waits for clear-sky days from Earth Engine
formulas.lead: A cloudy November and a quiet November can produce the same low count. Satellites cannot see fires through cloud, so FIREWORK divides the fire cell-days by the number of cell-days the satellite actually had a clear look. The result is burning per look, not burning per calendar day.
formulas.reads: The rate is fire cell-days divided by exposure, where exposure counts the cell-days on which the same platform's daily fire mask was a valid observation; with no valid observation the rate is unknown.

symbols.meaning: Fire cell-days of platform s in region r, month m
Exposure: cell-days with a valid observation by the same platform
Daily fire-mask class: 3 water, 5 clear land, 7–9 fire (low, nominal, high); 4 cloud and 6 unknown are not valid
Fire cell-days per valid observation

origin: Rates with an exposure denominator are the basis of epidemiology and of count models: events per person-year, accidents per vehicle-kilometre. In remote sensing the 'exposure' is the number of valid looks. NASA's daily fire masks classify every 1 km (MODIS) or 375 m (VIIRS) pixel every day as cloud, clear land, water or fire, which gives exactly the denominator FIREWORK needs.
why: Smoke and monsoon cloud are worst exactly when and where burning peaks. A raw count therefore undercounts the cloudiest months, and if cloudiness differs between years it can look like a trend. Dividing by exposure removes that artefact.
Exposure is also the correct offset in the count model (F14). Comparing MODIS and VIIRS per valid look, instead of per calendar day, separates 'sees fewer fires' from 'had fewer chances to look'.
On the Calendar the metric switch 'exposure rate' uses this formula; on the Brief it is listed as 'fire cell-days per valid day'.
how: For every cell, day and platform, the daily fire mask is valid when its class is 3, 5, 7, 8 or 9. Class 6 ('unknown') is not counted as clear. Summing valid cell-days over the region and month gives $E$. One valid day is one opportunity even if the satellite passed twice.
The rate is stored next to $E$, so the reader can always see how many looks a rate rests on. A rate built on very few looks is shown with its exposure and flagged.
example: Two Novembers with the same 600 fire cell-days. In a clear November the region offers 12,000 valid cell-days: $r = 600/12000 = 0.05$. In a cloudy November only 6,000: $r = 600/6000 = 0.10$. The second November burned twice as much per look, which the raw count hides.

For Punjab + Haryana the monthly VIIRS counts are in place (Novembers 2016–2025: 7,711, 6,068, 7,871, 4,572, 6,539, 9,603, 6,243, 5,928, 3,432, 2,157 cell-days); the clear-sky exposure is the pending input. Until it arrives the Calendar shows counts and labels the rate switch 'needs clear-sky days from Earth Engine'.

formulas.name: Monthly overlap ratio
formulas.status_text: Computed for every overlap month; feeds the diagnostics behind the calibration table
formulas.lead: Since 2012 MODIS and VIIRS have watched the same farms at the same time. For every month in that overlap, dividing the VIIRS count by the MODIS count gives one direct reading of how the two rulers relate. These monthly ratios are the raw evidence behind the exchange rate k.
equations: k_{r,\sigma,y} \;=\; \frac{V_{r,\sigma,y}}{M_{r,\sigma,y}}\qquad \text{for strata } \sigma \text{ where both sensors observed and } M>0
formulas.reads: For region r, stratum σ and year y, the overlap ratio is VIIRS cell-days divided by MODIS cell-days, computed only where both sensors have a valid value and MODIS is not zero.

symbols.meaning: VIIRS S-NPP fire cell-days
MODIS (Terra + Aqua) fire cell-days
Stratum: calendar month, and where available day/night and platform pair
Overlap year, 2012 onward
One reading of the VIIRS-to-MODIS ratio

origin: The ratio of two simultaneous measurements of the same quantity is the oldest way to cross-calibrate instruments; meteorologists use it to splice old and new rain gauges and satellite teams use it to link successive radiometers. It is valid only on the shared period and for like-with-like conditions, which is why FIREWORK computes it per stratum and only where both instruments were truly observing.
why: The harmonised calendar rests on one number per calendar month, k, and k must be justified by data the reader can see. The monthly ratios show whether k is stable from year to year, whether some years are odd, and how many years support it. The Sensor Lab bar chart of k by month is built from them.
Strata whose MODIS value is zero or missing cannot give a ratio. They are listed in a 'dropped' table rather than silently ignored, so nobody mistakes a missing month for agreement.
how: The pipeline joins the MODIS and S-NPP region-month tables on month, keeps months from 2012 on with valid status for both, and divides. Months with partial coverage are NULL and drop out with a reason. Ratios of small counts are lumpy (1 → 3 gives 3.0, 2 → 3 gives 1.5), so these readings are used for diagnosis and for the robust check (F11), while the published estimate pools them (F14).
example: November 2016: VIIRS 7,711 cell-days, MODIS 3,478, so $k = 7711/3478 = 2.22$.

Across fourteen Novembers the ratio stays between 1.53 and 2.49; October ratios run between 1.77 and 4.42, with the two highest in 2023 and 2024, when burning fell sharply and only the strongest fires remained visible to MODIS. Of 179 overlap months, 2 have no ratio: 2012-01, 2026-11 (partial download months).

formulas.name: Median of ratios
formulas.status_text: Computed as a robustness check beside the published ratio of totals
formulas.lead: One strange month should not move the exchange rate. The median of the monthly ratios is a robust second opinion on k: it ignores how big each month was and asks what a typical year looks like.
formulas.reads: The robust exchange rate is the median of the yearly ratios for a calendar month, using only years in which MODIS recorded at least five cell-days.

symbols.meaning: Overlap ratio for year y (F10)
MODIS cell-days that year
Minimum MODIS count for a ratio to be stable
Robust exchange rate

origin: The median is the classic robust estimator of location: up to half the values can be wild without moving it far. Robust ratio estimators of this kind are common in instrument intercomparison when a few periods are contaminated by outages or extreme events.
why: FIREWORK publishes k as a ratio of totals (F14) because that uses all the data with the right weights. The median of ratios checks that this pooled value is not driven by one or two huge months. Where the two agree, the reader can trust that k describes typical years; where they differ, the month needs a closer look.
The minimum of five MODIS cell-days removes ratios that are mostly noise: a month with one MODIS cell-day can give a ratio of 1 or of 12 by chance.
how: For each calendar month the yearly ratios with $M_y \ge 5$ are sorted and the middle value taken. With fewer than three usable years the result is 'insufficient' and the pooled value is used.

Because every year gets the same vote, the median weights a quiet year like a busy one. That is its strength against outliers and its weakness with sparse counts: in simulations with very small MODIS counts (0–3 per month) it underestimates k, which is why it is a check, not the default.
example: November, Punjab + Haryana: median of 14 yearly ratios = 2.14; ratio of totals = 2.10. October: 2.52 against 2.47. The two summaries agree to within a few percent in the burning season.
The largest gaps are in quiet months: January 6.02 against 5.49, June 6.14 against 5.43. There MODIS counts are small and single years swing widely, so the two estimators weigh them differently.

formulas.name: Harmonised MODIS value
formulas.status_text: Running in the pipeline: every pre-2012 month of the calendar has a harmonised value with a 95% band
formulas.lead: This is the formula that answers the challenge. MODIS months from before VIIRS existed are converted into VIIRS-equivalent units by multiplying by the exchange rate k for that calendar month. After 2012 the calendar shows what VIIRS actually observed. The 25-year record then sits on one ruler.
formulas.reads: Before 2012, the VIIRS-equivalent value for a month is the MODIS count times that calendar month's exchange rate, with a band from the ends of k's interval; from 2012 the observed VIIRS value is used.

symbols.meaning: MODIS fire cell-days in region r, calendar month m, year y
Exchange rate for that region and calendar month (F14)
95% interval of k from the year-block bootstrap (F24)
Harmonised, VIIRS-equivalent value (an estimate)

origin: Linear rescaling of an old instrument onto a new one, learned where both overlap, is how climate records are made continuous: sea-surface temperature from buckets to engine intakes, rainfall from old to new gauges. The exchange rate is fitted on the overlap and carried back, with an interval that says how sure we are.
why: Without harmonisation the calendar shows a jump at 2012 when VIIRS starts counting two to six times more cell-days. Any trend over 2000–2025 would mostly measure that switch. Converting MODIS into VIIRS units removes the instrument step while keeping MODIS's own year-to-year and seasonal pattern.

A separate k for each calendar month respects that the ratio depends on the season: small spring and winter fires are often missed by MODIS (k near 5), while the large rice-residue fires of October–November are seen by both (k near 2–2.5).
how: • Fit k for each calendar month on 2012 onward as the ratio of totals (F14), with a year-block bootstrap interval (F24).• For every year before 2012 multiply the MODIS value by k of its calendar month, and by the interval ends for the band.• From 2012 on, use the observed S-NPP value; its band is the value itself.• NULL stays NULL: a missing MODIS month is never multiplied.
The output is labelled as an estimate with its band and the k version used. It is a statement about what VIIRS would most likely have recorded, not a measurement.
example: November 2005: MODIS 2,332 cell-days. The November exchange rate is 2.096 [1.991, 2.198]. The harmonised value is $2.096 \times 2332 = 4888$ VIIRS-equivalent cell-days, with a 95% band from 4,643 to 5,126.

Figure 1 shows the October + November totals for every season. Raw MODIS before 2012 sits far below VIIRS after 2012; the harmonised series continues smoothly across the seam, and the shaded band shows the uncertainty carried from k.

formulas.name: Separate day and night factors
formulas.status_text: Computed from the cell-day table; shown on Sensor Lab as k day and k night
formulas.lead: Day and night detection work differently. At night the ground is cool, so small fires stand out, and VIIRS's finer pixels see far more of them than MODIS. Mixing day and night into one exchange rate hides that. FIREWORK computes k separately for each pass, using the real overpass times.
formulas.reads: For each region, calendar month and pass (day or night), the exchange rate is total VIIRS cell-days over total MODIS cell-days in that pass across the overlap years.

symbols.meaning: Pass: day (D) or night (N), from FIRMS daynight
Cell-days of each sensor in that pass
Pass-specific exchange rate

origin: Active-fire algorithms use different thresholds by day and night because reflected sunlight raises daytime background temperatures. NASA's product guides document that both sensors detect relatively more small fires at night, and that VIIRS's 375 m night detections are especially sensitive. Stratifying a calibration by such a known physical switch is standard practice.
why: Night burning matters for FIREWORK in two ways: industrial sources burn at night (F44), and a shift of crop burning toward evening would move fires away from the afternoon passes (F45). A single exchange rate dominated by daytime fires would badly underrate night activity in the harmonised record.

The overpass times also drift. Terra's morning crossing has moved earlier and Aqua's afternoon crossing later in recent years as their orbits decay. FIREWORK uses the observed acquisition times rather than nominal 10:30 and 13:30, so 'day' and 'night' strata are defined by what the satellites actually did.
how: The cell-day table already carries the pass of each detection. Summing MODIS and S-NPP cell-days separately for day and night, per calendar month over the overlap years, and dividing gives the two rates. Intervals come from the year-block bootstrap (F24). Night strata are sparse, so their intervals are wide and they are candidates for pooling (F18).

formulas.name: Poisson GLM with exposure offset
formulas.status_text: The live calibration is the intercept-only form (ratio of totals); the full model with exposure offsets runs once clear-sky days are loaded
formulas.lead: The exchange rate is best written as a count model: both sensors watch the same burning, each has its own sensitivity, and the number of looks enters as an offset. The model gives k as the difference of two sensor effects, and its simplest form is exactly the ratio of totals used on the live site.
equations: \hat k \;=\; e^{\hat\gamma_{V}-\hat\gamma_{M}}\qquad \text{intercept-only special case: }\ \hat k = \frac{\sum_t V_t}{\sum_t M_t}
formulas.reads: The expected count of sensor s in stratum t is the exposure times the shared activity of that stratum times the sensor's sensitivity; the exchange rate is the ratio of the two sensitivities.

symbols.meaning: Fire cell-days of sensor s in stratum t (a month of a year)
Exposure: valid observations of that sensor (F09); 1 until loaded
Latent burning activity shared by both sensors in stratum t
Sensitivity of sensor s
Negative-binomial dispersion (F15)
Exchange rate VIIRS : MODIS

origin: Generalised linear models with a log link and an offset were set out by Nelder and Wedderburn (1972) and are the standard tool for rates: deaths per person-year, claims per policy-year. In a paired design, where two instruments measure the same events, the shared term $\alpha_t$ absorbs everything both sensors see alike, and the sensor term $\gamma_s$ carries the systematic difference.
why: Writing k as a model, rather than just a ratio, does three things. It shows what is being assumed (both sensors see the same activity in a stratum). It allows exposure to enter properly, so a cloudier month for one sensor is not read as lower sensitivity. And it extends naturally: day/night, view angle or season can be added as covariates without inventing a new method.

It also clarifies a common confusion. With MODIS counts as the offset and only an intercept, the maximum-likelihood estimate of $e^{\beta}$ is exactly $\sum V/\sum M$. The GLM is then not an independent confirmation of the ratio of totals; it is the same estimator. Its value is in the extensions and the honest standard errors.
how: The pipeline currently publishes the intercept-only form for each calendar month: k is total VIIRS over total MODIS cell-days across the overlap years. When clear-sky exposure is loaded, the paired model is fitted with both sensors' counts stacked, a factor for every month-year ($\alpha_t$) and a sensor factor ($\gamma_s$), with $\log E$ as offset.

The Pearson dispersion of the fit decides the family: if it exceeds 1.5 the negative-binomial or quasi-Poisson form is used, which leaves k unchanged in the intercept-only case but widens its interval (F15).
example: November, 2012–2025: total VIIRS 89,005 and total MODIS 42,464 cell-days. Fitting $\log\mathbb{E}[V] = \log M + \beta$ gives $e^{\hat\beta} = 2.0960$, equal to the ratio of totals 2.0960.

The paired model over all 177 overlap months, with a factor per month-year and a sensor term, gives $\hat k = 2.562$, again equal to the pooled ratio 2.562. Its Pearson dispersion is 39.8, far above 1.5: real fire counts are much burstier than Poisson, so the Poisson standard error of log k (0.0034) is too small by a factor of about 6.3.

formulas.name: Negative-binomial variance
formulas.status_text: Dispersion is measured on every calibration fit; the NB form widens intervals where needed
formulas.lead: Fires come in bursts: a dry week, a harvest deadline or a ban lifted changes thousands of fields at once. A Poisson model assumes the spread of a count equals its mean, which real fire counts violate badly. The negative-binomial variance adds a second term that grows with the square of the mean.
formulas.reads: The variance of a negative-binomial count is its mean plus the mean squared over θ; the Pearson dispersion of a fitted model tells whether that extra term is needed.

symbols.meaning: Expected count
Dispersion: small θ means bursty counts; θ → ∞ gives Poisson
Pearson dispersion: 1 for Poisson data
Number of observations and fitted parameters

origin: The negative binomial arises when a Poisson rate itself varies randomly (a gamma-distributed rate): this is Greenwood and Yule's 1920 model of accident-prone workers. In ecology and epidemiology it is the default for clustered counts. The Pearson statistic is the standard check of whether a Poisson model's variance assumption holds.
why: Every interval FIREWORK shows rests on a variance. If counts are assumed Poisson when they are bursty, bands on k and on harmonised values come out too narrow and readers believe the record is more certain than it is. Measuring dispersion on the real fit, and switching to the NB form when it is large, keeps the bands honest.
The Validation page reports dispersion so that a reviewer can see why the intervals are as wide as they are.
how: After fitting the count model (F14), the pipeline computes $\hat\phi$. Values near 1 support Poisson. Values above 1.5 trigger the NB family or a quasi-Poisson scale, which multiplies standard errors by $\sqrt{\hat\phi}$. θ can be estimated by moments: $\hat\theta = \sum\mu_i^2 / \sum[(y_i-\mu_i)^2-\mu_i]$.
example: On the paired MODIS–VIIRS fit for Punjab + Haryana the Pearson dispersion is 39.8, so counts are far from Poisson. The moment estimate is $\hat\theta \approx 188$. For a month with μ = 2,332 cell-days the Poisson SD would be 48 while the NB SD is $\sqrt{2332 + 2332^2/188} = 177$.
A simple picture: with mean 100 and θ = 10, Var = 100 + 100²/10 = 1,100 and SD = 33, against SD = 10 for Poisson.

formulas.name: Delta-method interval for a ratio
formulas.status_text: Quick interval kept as an approximation; published bands use the year-block bootstrap
formulas.lead: A quick formula gives the uncertainty of a ratio of two counts. It is exact only if the two counts are independent and Poisson. For two sensors watching the same fires neither holds, so FIREWORK shows this interval as an approximation and publishes the bootstrap band instead.
formulas.reads: The variance of the log of a ratio is roughly one over each total, minus a term for their covariance; under independence the 95% interval is k times e to the power of plus or minus 1.96 standard errors.

symbols.meaning: Totals of VIIRS and MODIS cell-days
Covariance: positive, because both sensors see the same fires
Standard error of log k

origin: The delta method approximates the variance of a smooth function of random variables with a first-order Taylor expansion. For $\log(V/M) = \log V - \log M$ and Poisson counts, $\operatorname{Var}(\log V)\approx 1/V$. It is a standard result in survey sampling and epidemiology for rate ratios.
why: Readers deserve a quick sense of precision, and the delta method is the one most textbooks teach. FIREWORK keeps it, labelled 'approx.', because seeing why it fails is instructive: the covariance term is positive (shared fires narrow the interval), while over-dispersion (F15) widens it far more. The year-block bootstrap (F24) captures both without assuming either.
how: With totals $V$ and $M$, the standard error of $\log k$ is $\sqrt{1/V + 1/M}$ under independence and the interval is $k\,e^{\pm 1.96\,\mathrm{se}}$. When either total is zero the formula is undefined and returns nothing; exact Poisson bounds (F26) apply to each count instead.
example: November: V = 89,005, M = 42,464, k = 2.096. se = $\sqrt{1/89005 + 1/42464} = 0.0059$, so the delta interval is [2.072, 2.120]. The year-block bootstrap gives [1.991, 2.198], about 4 times wider.
The same holds every month (Figure 1). Big totals make the delta interval look extremely precise, but the years differ far more than Poisson noise would allow.

formulas.name: Shrink local factor toward global
formulas.status_text: Fallback rule for small areas; the data-driven version is F18
formulas.lead: A small region with a few noisy months can produce an extreme exchange rate. This rule pulls the local value toward a global one by a fixed amount of 'prior years', so small samples borrow strength and large samples keep their own value.
formulas.reads: The shrunk exchange rate is a weighted average of the local and the global value, where the local value counts once per year of data and the global value counts as n-nought extra years.

symbols.meaning: Exchange rate from the local data (region or month)
Exchange rate pooled over all data
Years of local data
Prior strength: how many years the global value is worth

origin: This is a credibility weighting, used by actuaries since the early twentieth century to blend a small portfolio's experience with the market average. It is also the posterior mean of a simple Bayesian model in which the global value is a prior worth $n_0$ observations.
why: FIREWORK aims to work on any region on Earth. Some will have only a few years of overlap or very few MODIS fires, and their raw k would swing widely. A shrink rule gives a stable value that moves toward the local evidence as it accumulates. It is transparent and easy to explain, which is why it is kept as the fallback when there are too few regions to estimate pooling from data (F18 needs at least three).
how: Each year of local data counts as one unit, the global value counts as $n_0$ units, and the result is the weighted average. With $n_0 = 4$ and 14 overlap years, a month keeps 78% of its own value. A region with 2 years keeps only 33%.
example: Shrinking each calendar month of Punjab + Haryana toward the all-month value 2.56 with $n_0 = 4$: September moves from 6.11 to 5.37, August from 1.49 to 1.72, November from 2.10 to 2.20.

Here the shrinkage is only for illustration: calendar months differ for physical reasons (season, fire size), so a single global value is not the right target for them. In use, the targets are other regions in the same calendar month.

formulas.name: Empirical Bayes partial pooling of log k
formulas.status_text: In the reference library; applied when at least three regions share a stratum
formulas.lead: Instead of fixing how much a region borrows from the group, partial pooling lets the data decide. Regions whose k is precise keep it; regions whose k is noisy move toward the group mean. The between-region variance τ² sets the balance.
equations: y_r = \log\hat k_r,\quad s_r^2 = \widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(y_r),\quad Q = \sum_r w_r (y_r-\bar y_w)^2,\quad w_r = 1/s_r^2
formulas.reads: Each region's log exchange rate is averaged with the group mean, keeping a share B that is large when the region's own estimate is precise compared with the spread between regions.

symbols.meaning: Log exchange rate of group r
Its sampling variance (from the bootstrap band)
Cochran's heterogeneity statistic
Between-group variance (DerSimonian–Laird)
Precision-weighted group mean with weights 1/(s²+τ²)
Share of a group's own value kept
Number of groups; at least 3

origin: The estimator for τ² is DerSimonian and Laird's 1986 method from meta-analysis, where results of several studies are combined. Shrinking each estimate toward the mean by $B_r$ is the empirical Bayes estimator of Efron and Morris (1975), famous for predicting baseball batting averages better than each player's own record.
why: FIREWORK fits k region by region. Regions differ for real reasons (fire sizes, crop types, cloud), so a single global k would be wrong, but some regions have far too little data for their own k. Partial pooling sits between those extremes and chooses the balance from the data, region by region. The Calendar inspector reports the share of own data used.
how: • Take each group's log k and its variance from the bootstrap.• Compute the fixed-effect mean and Cochran's Q.• Estimate τ²; if Q is below its expectation, τ² is 0 and all groups pool fully (reported).• Compute each group's kept share $B_r$ and the pooled log k; back-transform with exp.• With fewer than three groups, return nothing and fall back to F17.
example: Only one region is processed so far, so the method is shown with the twelve calendar months of Punjab + Haryana as the groups. Cochran's Q = 800.0 on 11 degrees of freedom, so the months differ far more than sampling noise: τ² = 0.202. Each month keeps most of its own value: November 99.7% (2.096 → 2.1), August, the noisiest month, 85.6% (1.489 → 1.69).

The outcome is the expected one: with precise months and a large real spread, pooling changes little. In a new region with two or three years of overlap, $s_r^2$ is large and $B_r$ small, and the region leans on the group.

formulas.code:
def eb_log_k(y, s2):
    y, s2 = np.asarray(y), np.asarray(s2)
    if len(y) < 3:
        return None
    w = 1 / s2
    q = np.sum(w * (y - np.sum(w * y) / w.sum()) ** 2)
    c = w.sum() - np.sum(w ** 2) / w.sum()
    tau2 = max(0.0, (q - (len(y) - 1)) / c)
    mu = np.sum(y / (s2 + tau2)) / np.sum(1 / (s2 + tau2))
    b = tau2 / (tau2 + s2)
    return b * y + (1 - b) * mu, b, tau2
references: DerSimonian, R., Laird, N. (1986). Meta-analysis in clinical trials. Controlled Clinical Trials 7, 177–188.
Efron, B., Morris, C. (1975). Data analysis using Stein's estimator and its generalizations. JASA 70, 311–319.
Cochran, W. G. (1954). The combination of estimates from different experiments. Biometrics 10.

formulas.name: Power law vs ratio (model choice)
formulas.status_text: Run as a held-out model test on every calibration; the live calendar uses the ratio per calendar month
formulas.lead: Is VIIRS simply a fixed multiple of MODIS, or does the multiple change with the size of the month? A power law lets the relation bend. FIREWORK decides between the two shapes by how well each predicts years it has not seen.
formulas.reads: Both models predict VIIRS from MODIS with a level for each calendar month; the ratio fixes the slope on the log scale at one, the power law estimates it; the winner has the lower Poisson deviance on held-out years.

symbols.meaning: Elasticity: % change in V for 1% change in M; b = 1 means proportional
Level for calendar month m
Small constant so empty MODIS months have a finite log
Poisson deviance, the count-data measure of misfit
Prediction for year y from a model fitted without year y

origin: Power laws are the simplest curved relation on a log–log plot. Choosing between nested models by out-of-sample deviance, rather than by in-sample fit, follows the cross-validation tradition (Stone, 1974) and the warning in Burnham and Anderson that model choice should target prediction.
why: If MODIS saturates in big fire months (many adjacent fires merge into one MODIS pixel while VIIRS still separates them), the true multiple would rise as months get bigger, and a single ratio would bias the harmonised peaks. If MODIS instead misses proportionally more in quiet months, the multiple falls with size. A held-out comparison tells which shape the data support and by how much.
how: For each overlap year: fit both models on the other years, predict the hidden year, and add up the Poisson deviance. The ratio model is the live calibration (one k per calendar month); the power law adds one parameter. If the power law improves held-out deviance by less than 2%, the simpler ratio is kept.
example: On Punjab + Haryana, 2012–2026, leaving out one year at a time (15 folds), the held-out deviance is 12,132 for the ratio and 7,812 for the power law, 35.6% lower. The fitted elasticity is $b = 0.73$ (range 0.68–0.75 across folds).

So the multiple is not constant: months with more MODIS activity have a smaller VIIRS : MODIS ratio, consistent with VIIRS keeping more of the small fires that dominate quiet months. This is a result FIREWORK reports alongside the ratio-based calendar; adopting the curved form for the published calendar is gated by the validation tests (F23, F35, F36).

formulas.name: Detection-probability curve (FRP₅₀)
formulas.status_text: Fitted on matched Aqua–S-NPP pairs; shown on Sensor Lab as the detection curve
formulas.lead: Why does VIIRS see more fires? Because MODIS misses small ones. Matching fires that both satellites passed over within minutes, this curve gives the probability that MODIS detects a fire of a given strength, and the strength at which it detects half of them: FRP₅₀.
formulas.reads: The log-odds that MODIS also detects a fire rise in a straight line with the logarithm of the fire's radiative power measured by VIIRS; the power at which the probability reaches one half is FRP-fifty.

symbols.meaning: 1 if Aqua MODIS detected the same fire, else 0
Fire radiative power measured by S-NPP VIIRS
Logistic intercept and slope
Strength at which MODIS detects 50% of fires

origin: Detection-probability curves come from sensor science and ecology (the probability of detecting an animal or a signal as a function of its strength). For fire, Schroeder et al. (2014) and later studies compared near-simultaneous MODIS and VIIRS observations to show that VIIRS detects many low-FRP fires that MODIS misses. Aqua and S-NPP fly in the same afternoon constellation, often minutes apart, which makes matched pairs possible.
why: The exchange rate k is a summary; this curve is the mechanism. It shows that k depends on the fire-size mix of a region and season: where fires are small (spring, winter, smallholder farms) MODIS misses more and k is larger; where fires are big, k is closer to 1. It also warns that k learned in one region may not transfer to another with different fires, which is why FIREWORK fits k per region and month.
how: • Take S-NPP daytime detections with FRP on days when Aqua passed within 15 minutes.• For each, look for an Aqua detection within 1.5 km (MODIS geolocation and pixel size).• Fit a logistic regression of 'Aqua detected' on ln FRP of the VIIRS fire.• Report FRP₅₀ = $e^{-\beta_0/\beta_1}$ and the curve.
FRP is skewed (F21), so the logarithm is the natural scale: each doubling of strength adds the same amount to the log-odds.
example: From 300,766 S-NPP daytime fires in Punjab + Haryana, 2012–2025, with Aqua overhead within 15 minutes, Aqua detected 22%. The fit gives $\beta_0 = -2.52$, $\beta_1 = 0.71$, so $\mathrm{FRP}_{50} = e^{2.52/0.71} = 35.6$ MW.
The median VIIRS fire in the sample has 5.3 MW, well below FRP₅₀. That is the core reason for k ≈ 2–6 in this region: most crop-residue fires are too weak for MODIS's 1 km pixel to register reliably.

formulas.name: Log transform of FRP
formulas.status_text: Used for FRP charts, z-scores and models wherever FRP is summarised
formulas.lead: Fire radiative power spans from under 1 MW for a small field to over 1,000 MW for an industrial flare. Averages of such numbers are ruled by a few giants. Taking the logarithm turns the long tail into a near-symmetric shape that charts and models handle well.
formulas.reads: The transformed value is the natural logarithm of one plus the fire radiative power measured in megawatts.

symbols.meaning: Fire radiative power of a detection
Log-scaled FRP; zero at FRP = 0

origin: Fire radiative power is retrieved from the 4 µm radiance excess of a fire pixel (Wooster et al., 2003). Its distribution is close to log-normal, as many environmental magnitudes are. The '+1' keeps zero defined; dividing by 1 MW makes the units explicit so the transform does not change if FRP is ever stored in watts.
why: FIREWORK shows FRP on Explorer and uses it as a feature for source attribution and in the detection curve (F20). Without the log, a single refinery flare would dominate every mean and every colour scale, and statistical tests that assume rough symmetry would mislead.
how: Each FRP value in megawatts is shifted by one and logged. Missing or negative FRP stays NULL. FRP is compared only within a sensor: MODIS and VIIRS retrieve it from different pixel sizes and bands, so their FRP values differ systematically (F22).
example: S-NPP in Punjab + Haryana: median FRP 4.9 MW, mean 6.7 MW, maximum 296.8 MW. MODIS: median 12.8 MW, maximum 1,104.7 MW. The skewness of S-NPP FRP falls from 5.0 to 0.7 after the transform.
A 1,000 MW detection becomes $\ln(1001) = 6.909$; a 5 MW fire becomes $\ln 6 = 1.79$.

formulas.name: Quantile mapping (FRP only)
formulas.status_text: Available on Sensor Lab's advanced tab for FRP distributions; never applied to counts
formulas.lead: Counts get one exchange rate, but FRP is a whole distribution. Quantile mapping translates a MODIS FRP value into the VIIRS value at the same rank: the MODIS median becomes the VIIRS median, the MODIS 90th percentile becomes the VIIRS 90th percentile.
formulas.reads: To map a MODIS value x, find its cumulative share among MODIS values, then read the VIIRS value with the same cumulative share.

symbols.meaning: A MODIS FRP value
Empirical cumulative distribution of MODIS and VIIRS FRP on the overlap
VIIRS quantile function (inverse CDF)
MODIS value expressed on the VIIRS FRP scale

origin: Quantile mapping is the workhorse of climate-model bias correction (Panofsky and Brier, 1968; widely used since the 2000s) and of histogram matching in image processing. It aligns whole distributions, not just means.
why: Because MODIS pixels are larger and miss weak fires, MODIS FRP values are higher on average than VIIRS values for the same season. To show FRP distributions across 25 years on one scale, the shapes must be aligned. Quantile mapping does that for FRP. It is deliberately not used for counts, because forcing an old period's distribution to look like the new period's would erase real changes in the tails.
how: On the overlap period and within a stratum (here October–November daytime, Aqua against S-NPP), FIREWORK builds both empirical CDFs. A MODIS value is converted to its CDF rank and the VIIRS quantile at that rank is read off. Values outside the training range are flagged as extrapolations.
example: October–November daytime, 2012–2025: Aqua median FRP 12.5 MW (182,239 detections), S-NPP median 5.0 MW (873,494 detections). The mapping sends the Aqua median to 5.0 MW, an Aqua 50 MW fire to 22.3 MW and an Aqua 10 MW fire to 4.0 MW.
Above the Aqua 99th percentile (70.6 MW) values are outside the training range and are flagged rather than mapped.

formulas.name: Bland–Altman agreement
formulas.status_text: Computed on held-out years; Validation gate G7 requires |bias| ≤ 0.1
formulas.lead: Correlation tells whether two series move together; it does not tell whether they agree. Bland–Altman analysis measures agreement directly: the average difference (bias) between harmonised MODIS and observed VIIRS, and the range within which 95% of differences fall.
formulas.reads: For each held-out month the difference is the log of the harmonised MODIS value minus the log of the observed VIIRS value; the bias is their mean and the limits of agreement are the mean plus or minus 1.96 standard deviations.

symbols.meaning: Harmonised MODIS, $\hat k_{-y} M_t$, with k fitted without that year
Observed VIIRS S-NPP
Log difference: positive when harmonised MODIS is higher
Bias
Limits of agreement

origin: Bland and Altman (1986) introduced the method in The Lancet to compare two ways of measuring the same clinical quantity, after showing that correlation is misleading for that purpose. It is now standard in method-comparison studies in medicine and remote sensing. Counts have spread that grows with size, so FIREWORK works on the log scale, where differences are ratios.
why: The Validation page must show that harmonised MODIS can stand in for VIIRS. Agreement on the very years used to fit k would be circular, so each year is held out in turn: k is fitted on the other years and applied to the hidden year's MODIS value, which is then compared with what VIIRS really recorded.
how: For each overlap year, for each month, compute $a_t$ from the leave-one-year-out k and $b_t$ from observation, take the log difference, and summarise. With fewer than eight points the limits are not drawn. The sign convention is fixed: $a - b$, harmonised minus observed.
example: All 177 held-out overlap months: bias $\bar d = -0.046$ (harmonised MODIS 4.5% lower than VIIRS on average), SD 0.40, limits of agreement [-0.84, +0.74], meaning a harmonised month lies between 0.43× and 2.10× the observed value 95% of the time.

formulas.name: Block bootstrap over years
formulas.status_text: Running in the pipeline: every k in the calibration table has a 95% year-block bootstrap interval (B = 2,000)
formulas.lead: How sure are we about k? Resample whole years of the overlap with replacement, recompute k each time, and read the middle 95% of the results. Resampling years, not months, respects that months within a year share the same weather, policy and harvest.

formulas.reads: Draw a new set of years with replacement, recompute the ratio of totals, repeat two thousand times, and take the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles as the 95% interval.

Exchange rate in bootstrap sample b
Number of bootstrap samples

origin: Efron's bootstrap (1979) estimates uncertainty by resampling the data. Künsch (1989) extended it to dependent data by resampling blocks; here a block is one year of the calendar month. The percentile interval is the simplest bootstrap interval and works well for smooth statistics such as a ratio of sums.
why: Real fire counts are over-dispersed and correlated within years, so the textbook formula for a ratio's interval (F16) is far too narrow. The year-block bootstrap makes no Poisson assumption: if some years are odd, the interval widens in proportion. It is the band shown with every k on the Calendar inspector and Sensor Lab, and it propagates into the harmonised band (F12).
how: • For one calendar month, list the overlap years with their MODIS and VIIRS totals.• Draw as many years as there are, with replacement.• Recompute k as the ratio of the summed totals (summing first avoids dividing by a zero year).• Repeat B = 2,000 times with a fixed seed for reproducibility.• Report the 2.5% and 97.5% quantiles and state the level.
example: November, Punjab + Haryana: 14 overlap years, k = 2.096. The 95% interval is [1.992, 2.209]; the 90% interval is [2.009, 2.187]. The value stored in the calibration table, from the pipeline's own run, is [1.991, 2.198]; the small difference is bootstrap randomness.

formulas.name: Monte Carlo error propagation
formulas.status_text: In the reference library; the Calendar band shows k uncertainty, this adds count noise for predictive bands
formulas.lead: A harmonised month carries two kinds of uncertainty: how well we know k, and how bursty the MODIS count itself is. Simulation combines them honestly: draw k, draw the count, multiply, repeat, and read the spread.
formulas.reads: Draw the exchange rate on the log scale around its estimate, draw a count from a negative binomial around the observed MODIS value, multiply them, and repeat many times; the middle 95% of the products is the predictive band.

symbols.meaning: Standard error of log k (from the bootstrap band)
NB dispersion of counts
One simulated harmonised value
Number of draws (20,000)

origin: Propagating uncertainty by simulation is the Monte Carlo method of the GUM Supplement 1 (JCGM 101, 2008), the international guide to measurement uncertainty. It replaces linear error formulas when quantities multiply, are skewed or must stay positive.
why: The Calendar band currently reflects uncertainty in k only: it answers 'how sure are we of the expected value?'. A user asking 'what range could VIIRS actually have recorded that month?' needs a predictive band that also includes count noise. Both have a place; FIREWORK labels which one is shown. Drawing k on the log scale guarantees positive multipliers; a normal draw on the raw scale with a large spread produces negative k.
how: Draw 20,000 values of log k from a normal with the bootstrap-derived standard error and exponentiate. Draw 20,000 MODIS counts from a negative binomial with the observed mean and the fitted θ. Multiply pairwise and take quantiles. Do not add count noise twice: the bootstrap of k already contains count noise of the overlap years, but not of the target month.
example: November 2005: M = 2,332, k = 2.096, se(log k) = 0.025, θ = 188. The calibration-only 95% band is [4,655, 5,141]; the predictive band, adding count noise, is [4,166, 5,697] around a median of 4,885.
All draws are positive. For contrast, drawing k from a normal with mean 2.10 and SD 1.5 would give negative multipliers in 8.2% of draws.

formulas.name: Exact Poisson interval (Garwood)
formulas.status_text: Used for small counts (0–10) on cell and month inspectors
formulas.lead: When a cell or a month has only a handful of fire cell-days, the usual 'plus or minus 1.96 square-root' shortcut breaks: it goes below zero and gives no interval at all for zero. The Garwood interval is exact for Poisson counts and stays correct down to zero.
formulas.reads: The interval for the true rate behind an observed count n runs from half the chi-square quantile with 2n degrees of freedom to half the chi-square quantile with 2n + 2 degrees of freedom.

symbols.meaning: Observed count
p-quantile of the chi-square distribution with ν degrees of freedom
1 − coverage, 0.05

origin: Garwood (1936) derived the interval by inverting the Poisson tail probabilities; the link to the chi-square distribution follows from the relation between Poisson and gamma distributions. It is 'exact' in the sense that its coverage is never below the nominal level.
why: Small counts are everywhere in FIREWORK: quiet months, small regions, single cells on the Explorer inspector, the summer months of the Terra-only years. Showing '0 ± 0' for an empty month would claim certainty that no fire happened; the Garwood interval says the true rate is between 0 and 3.7, which is the honest statement.
how: Look up two chi-square quantiles and halve them. For n = 0 the lower bound is 0 and the upper is $-\ln(0.025) = 3.69$. The interval is slightly conservative: its coverage is at least 95%.
example: n = 0 → [0, 3.69]. n = 3 → [0.62, 8.77], where the normal shortcut gives [-0.40, 6.39] with a negative lower end. n = 10 → [4.79, 18.39].
In Punjab + Haryana 9% of MODIS months have 10 or fewer fire cell-days; July and August of the early 2000s are typical examples.

from scipy.stats import chi2
def garwood(n, alpha=0.05):
    lo = 0.0 if n == 0 else chi2.ppf(alpha / 2, 2 * n) / 2
    hi = chi2.ppf(1 - alpha / 2, 2 * n + 2) / 2
    return lo, hi

garwood(3)   # (0.619, 8.767)
references: Garwood, F. (1936). Fiducial limits for the Poisson distribution. Biometrika 28, 437–442.

formulas.name: Robust anomaly z-score
formulas.status_text: Running in the pipeline: anomaly.csv holds z, the reference median and the number of reference years for every month
formulas.lead: Is this November unusual? The robust z-score compares a month with the same calendar month in every other year, on a log scale, using the median and the median absolute deviation so that one extreme year cannot distort the yardstick. The month being judged is left out of its own baseline.
formulas.reads: Take the log of the month's value, subtract the median log value of the same month in the other years, and divide by the robust spread of those years, never less than 0.15; at least eight reference years are required for a full result.

symbols.meaning: Value of the target month on the harmonised scale (hot spots or cell-days; rate once exposure exists)
Reference set: the same calendar month in all other years
Median
Median absolute deviation from the median
Makes MAD comparable to a standard deviation for normal data
Floor on the spread, so near-identical years do not give huge z
Robust anomaly: how many robust spreads above or below normal

origin: The z-score is the standard way to express an anomaly. Replacing mean and standard deviation by median and MAD (Hampel, 1974) makes it robust to outliers; the factor 1.4826 is $1/\Phi^{-1}(0.75)$. Leaving the target out of its own baseline is the leave-one-out principle: an extreme month should not soften its own yardstick. The log with +0.5 is an Anscombe-style variance stabiliser for counts and keeps zero finite.
why: The Calendar's anomaly view and the Brief both answer 'how unusual is this month?'. Raw counts cannot answer it: the October–November peak is hundreds of times larger than July. Comparing a month only with the same calendar month, on a log scale, puts every month on the same footing, and the robust statistics keep one record-breaking year from hiding the next one.
Because the comparison runs on the harmonised scale, a pre-2012 month and a post-2012 month are compared on one ruler, which is the point of the challenge.
how: • Take the target month's harmonised value and the same calendar month in every other year.• Log all values with +0.5.• Median and MAD of the reference logs; spread = max(1.4826·MAD, 0.15).• z = (target log − median) / spread.• Status 'ok' with eight or more reference years, 'indicative' below; missing months are excluded, not treated as zero.
example: November 2025 in Punjab + Haryana: 3,413 hot spots (VIIRS-equivalent). The 25 other Novembers have a median of 28,101, so the month is 88% below normal. On the log scale the reference median is 10.24 and the robust spread is 0.72, giving $z = -2.93$.

The most negative months in the record are 2026-10 (z = -8.2), 2025-10 (z = -7.5), 2000-11 (z = -6.5): the collapse of residue burning since 2023 is the largest anomaly in 26 years. The most positive are 2004-09 (z = 4.5), 2006-09 (z = 4.2), 2001-09 (z = 3.5), early Septembers with unusual early burning.

formulas.name: Season start, peak and end (10 / 90%)
formulas.status_text: In the reference library; drawn on the Calendar as the season band
formulas.lead: When does the burning season open, peak and close? Within a declared window, the season starts when 10% of the window's detected activity has happened, ends at 90%, and peaks in the busiest week. These are dates of detected activity, which is what satellites can tell us.
equations: w_{\mathrm{peak}} = \arg\max_w\ c_w,\qquad \text{NULL if any week is unobserved}
formulas.reads: Add up weekly fire cell-days through the window; the season starts in the first week where the running total reaches 10% of the window's total, ends where it reaches 90%, and peaks in the week with the most.

symbols.meaning: Fire cell-days in week w (one sensor, e.g. VIIRS S-NPP)
Cumulative cell-days up to week w
Total in the window
Declared season window
Season dates

origin: Percentile-based phenology is used for growing seasons (for example the start of season at 10% of the annual vegetation-index rise) and for fire seasons in global fire climatologies (Giglio et al., 2006). Using cumulative shares rather than a fixed count threshold makes the dates comparable between big and small years.
why: The challenge asks for the critical period of burning. Farmers, regulators and health agencies need to know whether the residue-burning season is arriving earlier or later and whether its end is moving into the colder weeks of November, when smoke traps more easily. These dates turn the calendar into a schedule.
how: Use one consistent sensor for all years (VIIRS S-NPP from 2012), declare the window for the season (kharif residue: 15 September – 31 December in Punjab + Haryana), sum cell-days by week, and read off the 10% and 90% weeks and the busiest week. A second window (for example April–May for wheat residue) gives the other season. A week without observation makes the year NULL.
example: Punjab + Haryana, VIIRS S-NPP, kharif window: 2012 06 Oct → 23 Nov (peak 27 Oct); 2016 06 Oct → 23 Nov (peak 27 Oct); 2020 06 Oct → 23 Nov (peak 27 Oct); 2024 06 Oct → 30 Nov (peak 27 Oct); 2025 13 Oct → 30 Nov (peak 03 Nov).

The season is remarkably stable in timing, opening in the first half of October and closing in the second half of November, while its size fell from 18,231 cell-days in 2016 to 4,010 in 2025. In the most recent years the end has moved a week later and the peak toward early November.

formulas.name: Mann–Kendall trend test
formulas.status_text: In the reference library; drawn as the Calendar trend line with its p-value
formulas.lead: Is burning rising or falling over the years? The Mann–Kendall test counts, for every pair of years, whether the later one is higher or lower. It needs no straight line and no normal errors, which suits fire counts.
formulas.reads: Score +1 for every pair of years where the later is higher and −1 where it is lower; standardise the sum with its variance, corrected for ties, and read a two-sided p-value from the normal curve.

symbols.meaning: Season total in year i (harmonised)
Kendall score: positive = rising
Size of each group of tied values
Standardised score and two-sided p-value

origin: Mann (1945) proposed the test and Kendall (1975) gave its distribution; it is the standard non-parametric trend test in hydrology and climatology. The tie correction matters for counts, where equal values (especially zeros) are common.
why: A trend is the headline many users want: is stubble burning declining? Mann–Kendall answers on ranks, so one extreme year cannot manufacture a trend. Run on the harmonised series, it is not fooled by the 2012 jump, which a raw MODIS-then-VIIRS series would read as a large rise.
how: Compute the sign of every pairwise difference, sum, compute the variance with the tie correction, standardise with the continuity correction and read p. Fewer than eight years are reported as 'too short'. Autocorrelation is handled by F31 and the size of the trend by F32.
example: October + November fire cell-days on the harmonised scale, 2001–2025 (n = 25): S = -48, Var(S) = 1,833.3, Z = -1.10, p = 0.272. Over the full 25 seasons there is no significant monotonic trend.

The series shows why: it rises from 2,265 in 2001 (Terra only) to a plateau of 14,000–17,000 cell-days from 2005 to 2021, then falls steeply to 3,479 in 2025. A rank test over the whole period sees roughly as many rising as falling pairs; the recent decline is a change in level (F33–F34), not a steady trend.

formulas.name: Hamed–Rao autocorrelation correction
formulas.status_text: In the reference library; applied with every Mann–Kendall result
formulas.lead: Neighbouring years are often alike: a wet year follows a wet year, a policy lasts several seasons. That makes a series look more certain than it is. The Hamed–Rao correction inflates the variance of the Mann–Kendall score by the effective loss of independent years.
formulas.reads: Multiply the Mann–Kendall variance by the ratio of the actual to the effective sample size, which grows with the significant autocorrelations of the detrended ranks.

symbols.meaning: Autocorrelation at lag k of the ranks of the detrended series (only significant lags)
Effective number of independent years
Corrected variance

origin: Hamed and Rao (1998) derived the correction in the Journal of Hydrology for streamflow series, where persistence is strong. It removes the trend first (Sen's slope), ranks the residuals and keeps only lags whose autocorrelation is significant at 5%.
why: Without it, a short positively autocorrelated series can show a 'significant' trend that is really a few long swings. FIREWORK reports raw and corrected p-values together so readers see when persistence matters.
how: Detrend with Sen's slope, rank the residuals, compute the autocorrelation at each lag, keep lags outside ±1.96/√n, compute n/n* and multiply the variance. Z and p are recomputed with the new variance.
example: For the 25-season series, the lag-1 and lag-2 autocorrelations of detrended ranks are 0.18 and 0.29, below the significance bound ±0.39. No lag is significant, so n/n* = 1.00 and the corrected p equals the raw p (0.272).
With only 25 years the autocorrelations are noisy; that is why the correction keeps only significant lags and why both p-values are shown.

formulas.name: Sen's slope
formulas.status_text: In the reference library; label of the Calendar trend line
formulas.lead: How fast is the series changing? Sen's slope takes the slope between every pair of years and reports the median. Like Mann–Kendall it is robust: a single extreme season barely moves it.
formulas.reads: The slope is the median, over all pairs of years, of the change in value divided by the number of years between them.

symbols.meaning: Value and year of observation i
Robust change per year

origin: Theil (1950) and Sen (1968) proposed the median of pairwise slopes; it tolerates up to about 29% outliers and pairs naturally with Mann–Kendall.
why: A p-value says whether a trend exists; the slope says how big it is. FIREWORK reports both, and expresses the slope as a percentage of the median level so regions of different sizes compare. Using real year gaps lets missing years be skipped without bias.
how: Compute $(x_j-x_i)/(t_j-t_i)$ for all pairs with both values present (300 pairs for 25 years) and take the median. A confidence interval comes from ranks of the pairwise slopes or from resampling.
example: October + November, harmonised, 2001–2025: Sen's slope = -114 cell-days per year over 300 pairs, or -0.79% of the median season (14,400) per year. Small relative to the collapse after 2022, which is a level change rather than a steady slope.
