formulas.name: Pettitt change-point test
formulas.status_text: Run in validation on raw and harmonised series; gate G4 uses placebo years
formulas.lead: Where is the single most likely jump in a series? Pettitt's test scans every possible split year. Run on the stitched raw record (MODIS then VIIRS) it should find the 2012 instrument seam; run on the harmonised record it should not.
formulas.reads: For each candidate split, compare every value before it with every value after it; the split with the largest absolute score is the change point, and its significance follows from the size of that score.

symbols.meaning: Mann–Whitney-type score for a split after year t
Largest absolute score
Approximate p-value

origin: Pettitt (1979) gave the non-parametric change-point test, widely used in hydrology to find shifts in rainfall and streamflow records. It is rank-based, so robust to skewed counts.
why: The purpose of harmonisation is to remove the 2012 step. Pettitt gives a direct before/after check. A non-significant result after harmonisation is necessary but not sufficient, because the test has low power with 25 points; FIREWORK pairs it with placebo years and the seam ratio (F35).
how: Compute $U_t$ for every split, take the maximum absolute value, and convert to p. Repeat at placebo years (random non-sensor years and the 2018 and 2023 platform additions) to estimate the false-alarm rate.
example: October + November season totals, 2001–2025. Stitched raw series: K = 122, change after 2011, p = 0.0082, which is the instrument seam at 2012. Harmonised series: K = 76, most likely split after 2017, p = 0.24, not significant. The seam is gone; the remaining weak split marks the start of the recent decline.

formulas.name: PELT multiple change points
formulas.status_text: Run in validation on monthly series; penalty fixed before running
formulas.lead: Instruments joined the record at several moments: Aqua in 2002, S-NPP in 2012, NOAA-20 in 2018, NOAA-21 in 2023. PELT finds every step in a series at once, with a penalty declared in advance so it cannot be tuned to tell a story.
formulas.reads: Split the deseasonalised log series into segments so that the total squared deviation from each segment's mean, plus a fixed penalty per extra segment, is as small as possible.

symbols.meaning: Change points
Segment cost: squared deviation from the segment mean
Penalty per change point (BIC-type), declared before running
Robust noise level from month-to-month differences

origin: PELT (Pruned Exact Linear Time) by Killick, Fearnhead and Eckley (2012) finds the exact optimal segmentation with a penalty, fast enough for long series. The squared-error cost on a log scale turns multiplicative sensor steps into shifts in the mean; the BIC-type penalty 2σ²ln n is the standard choice for a mean change.
why: Pettitt finds one break. The FIREWORK record could contain several instrument steps and real changes. PELT shows all of them, so the Validation page can say which steps harmonisation removed, which remain, and which are real changes in burning.
how: Take monthly values, log with +0.5, subtract each calendar month's median to remove the season, estimate the noise level robustly from successive differences, set β = 2σ²ln n, and run PELT with a minimum segment of 12 months.

The 2011–12 break, VIIRS joining, disappears after harmonisation. The early-2002 break remains in both: it is Aqua joining Terra in the MODIS family, a step inside MODIS that the MODIS-to-VIIRS calibration does not touch. FIREWORK reports it as a known residual seam.

formulas.name: Seam ratio
formulas.status_text: Computed in validation; gate G3 requires the upper interval ≤ 0.25
formulas.lead: How much of the 2012 instrument step is left after harmonisation? The seam ratio divides the step in the harmonised series by the step in the stitched raw series, using three-year windows on a log scale. Zero means the seam is gone; one means nothing was fixed.
formulas.reads: The seam ratio is the change in the mean log harmonised value across the 2012 seam divided by the change in the raw record across the same seam.

symbols.meaning: Harmonised season total
Raw VIIRS after and raw MODIS before the seam

origin: Comparing the size of a discontinuity before and after a correction is the core of homogenisation in climate records (for example the step tests of Alexandersson). Three-year windows and logs reduce the influence of a single year and of the multiplicative size of the step.
why: It turns 'the seam is fixed' into a number with an interval. Natural year-to-year change also exists, so FIREWORK compares the real seam with placebo seams at years where no instrument changed: a successful harmonisation leaves a seam no larger than ordinary change.
how: Compute mean logs in 2009–11 and 2012–14 for the harmonised and the stitched raw series and divide. Bootstrap years within each window for the interval. Repeat at placebo years with the same denominator to see the size of natural change.
example: October + November seasons: the raw step across 2012 is a factor of 2.30 (+130%). After harmonisation the step is 0.011 in log units, so $R_{\mathrm{seam}} = 0.011/0.832 = 0.013$, with a 95% interval [0.002, 0.100]. Placebo seams at other years have a median of 0.080: what remains at 2012 is smaller than ordinary year-to-year change. The upper interval is below the 0.25 gate.

formulas.status_text: Computed in validation; gate G1 requires median relative error ≤ 15% and better than a constant k
formulas.lead: The honest test of a calibration is a year it has never seen. Hide one overlap year, fit k on the rest, predict the hidden year's VIIRS value from its MODIS value, and measure the miss. Repeat for every year.

origin: Leave-one-out and blocked cross-validation are standard for honest error estimates (Stone, 1974; Roberts et al., 2017 for structured data). formulas.name: Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate
formulas.status_text: In the reference library; used for the Explorer trend map 'FDR 5%'
formulas.lead: Test a trend in 751 cells at the 5% level and about 38 will look significant by chance alone. The Benjamini–Hochberg procedure controls the share of false discoveries among the cells it marks, so a trend map does not light up with noise.
formulas.reads: Sort the p-values, find the largest rank whose p-value is below rank over m times α, and declare that many smallest p-values significant.

symbols.meaning: Number of cells actually tested (with enough data)
i-th smallest p-value
Target false discovery rate, 5%

origin: Benjamini and Hochberg (1995) introduced the false discovery rate, one of the most cited ideas in modern statistics. Under independence or positive dependence it keeps the expected share of false positives among discoveries at α. Benjamini and Yekutieli (2001) gave a variant for arbitrary dependence.
why: Explorer's trend map tests every cell. Without a multiple-testing rule, scattered 'significant' cells would appear even in a stable region and invite false stories. With BH, a marked cell is trustworthy at the stated rate.
how: Run Mann–Kendall on each cell's season series (cells with at least 20 fire cell-days), sort the p-values, apply the step-up rule, and colour only the rejected cells by the sign of their trend. Report m honestly.
example: Punjab + Haryana, VIIRS S-NPP October–November cell-days per cell, 2012–2025: m = 751 cells tested. 446 have p < 0.05 (about 38 would by chance), and 387 survive BH at 5%: 375 falling and 12 rising. The decline in residue burning is real across most of the agricultural plain.

formulas.code:
def benjamini_hochberg(p, alpha=0.05):
    p = np.asarray(p); m = len(p); order = np.argsort(p)
    ok = p[order] <= alpha * np.arange(1, m + 1) / m
    k = np.max(np.where(ok)[0]) + 1 if ok.any() else 0
    reject = np.zeros(m, bool); reject[order[:k]] = True
    return reject
references: Benjamini, Y., Hochberg, Y. (1995). Controlling the false discovery rate. JRSS B 57, 289–300.
Benjamini, Y., Yekutieli, D. (2001). The control of the false discovery rate in multiple testing under dependency. Annals of Statistics 29.

formulas.name: Kalman fusion (local-level model)
formulas.status_text: Experimental: shown on Sensor Lab's experimental tab; never presented as observed
formulas.lead: With two sensors overlapping since 2012, which one should the record follow? A Kalman filter blends them month by month, trusting each in proportion to its precision, and carries a smooth estimate of the underlying activity through gaps.
equations: x_t = x_{t-1} + w_t,\quad w_t\sim\mathcal N(0,Q);\qquad z_{s,t} = x_t + v_{s,t},\quad v_{s,t}\sim\mathcal N(0,R_s)
formulas.reads: The hidden level wanders a little each month; each sensor measures it with its own noise; the filter predicts, then corrects toward each available measurement with a gain that is large when the sensor is precise.

symbols.meaning: Underlying activity level (deseasonalised log cell-days)
Measurement by sensor s: harmonised MODIS or VIIRS
Process noise: how fast the level can change
Measurement noise of sensor s
Kalman gain

origin: Kalman's 1960 filter is the optimal linear estimator for a linear Gaussian state-space model; the local-level model is its simplest case (Durbin and Koopman, 2012). It is used from spacecraft navigation to sea-surface temperature blending.
why: Sensor fusion is an optional layer of FIREWORK: it shows how a single best estimate could combine all instruments. It is experimental because its result is a model estimate, so it is labelled and never shown as an observation.
how: Work on deseasonalised logs. Start from the first valid measurement. Each month: add Q to the uncertainty, then update with each available sensor in turn; skip missing values. Measurement noise comes from validation: harmonised MODIS SD 0.40 (Bland–Altman, F23), VIIRS 0.12.
example: With Q = 0.02, R_MODIS = 0.40² and R_VIIRS = 0.12², the gain on harmonised MODIS before 2012 settles at about 0.23: each new MODIS month moves the estimate by about a fifth of its surprise. After 2012 VIIRS dominates because it is much more precise, and the fused level follows it closely while MODIS still pulls slightly.

origin: Conformal prediction (Vovk, Gammerman and Shafer, 2005) gives distribution-free coverage guarantees under exchangeability; split conformal (Papadopoulos et al., 2002; Angelopoulos and Bates, 2021) does so with one calibration set.
why: Source attribution is uncertain by nature, and a single label would overstate it. A set with a coverage guarantee lets the Sources page say 'crop or kiln' honestly and abstain when the set has more than one member.

formulas.name: Haversine distance
formulas.status_text: Used for matching sensors, clustering and context distances
formulas.lead: Degrees are not kilometres: one degree of longitude is 111 km at the equator but 96 km over Punjab. The haversine formula gives the great-circle distance between two points on the sphere, which FIREWORK uses whenever it asks 'how far?'.
formulas.reads: The distance is twice the Earth's radius times the arcsine of the square root of the haversine of the latitude difference plus the cosines of both latitudes times the haversine of the longitude difference.

symbols.meaning: Latitudes
Differences in latitude and longitude
Mean Earth radius (as in F04)
Great-circle distance

origin: The haversine form of the spherical law of cosines was popular in navigation because it stays accurate for small distances; Sinnott (1984) recommended it for computers. On a sphere its error against the ellipsoid is below about 0.3%.
why: Matching an S-NPP fire to an Aqua fire (F20), clustering detections into sites (F41) and measuring distance to industry (F42) all need distances in kilometres, consistent with the cell areas of F04.
how: Convert degrees to radians, compute the haversine terms, take the arcsine. For sub-kilometre precision the geodesic on the ellipsoid (Karney) is available; for FIREWORK's scales the sphere suffices.
example: Ludhiana (30.901°N, 75.857°E) to Amritsar (31.634°N, 74.872°E): d = 124.1 km. One degree of longitude at 30.5°N is 95.8 km against 111.2 km at the equator.

In the matched-pair analysis, the distance from each S-NPP fire to the nearest Aqua fire on the same overpass has a median of 1.08 km among pairs within 3 km (107,787 pairs), consistent with MODIS pixel size and geolocation.

formulas.name: DBSCAN fire clustering (space and time)
formulas.status_text: In the reference library; builds the sites used by persistence and night share
formulas.lead: Detections that sit close together in space and time usually belong to one burning event or one site. DBSCAN groups them without being told how many groups to expect. Adding a time window keeps fires on different days from merging into one giant cluster.

origin: DBSCAN (Ester, Kriegel, Sander and Xu, 1996) is a density-based clustering algorithm that finds clusters of any shape and labels noise. ST-DBSCAN (Birant and Kut, 2007) adds a temporal neighbourhood.
why: Persistence (F08) and night share (F44) are properties of sites, not of single pixels. Clusters also turn thousands of points into a manageable number of events for the Sources page. A cluster is not a count of fires; it is a grouping for analysis.
how: Project points to kilometres, find pairs within ε_s, keep pairs within ε_t days, and run DBSCAN on this neighbourhood graph with minPts = 3. Points not in any cluster are noise. ε is set per sensor because geolocation differs.

formulas.name: Distance-decay exposure (IE / AE)
formulas.status_text: Defined; waits for mapped industrial and cropland features (OpenStreetMap, land cover) per region
formulas.lead: How much industry surrounds a fire, and how much cropland? Each nearby feature contributes a weight that fades with distance. Summing them gives an industrial exposure IE and an agricultural exposure AE for every site.
formulas.reads: Industrial exposure is the sum over industrial features of their weight times an exponential that falls with distance; agricultural exposure is the same over cropland.

origin: Exponential distance decay is standard in spatial interaction models and in exposure science (for example traffic-pollution exposure). It gives near features more influence without a hard cut-off.
why: A hot spot next to a refinery is more likely industrial; one in the middle of paddy fields is more likely crop residue. IE and AE give the source classifier this context as smooth numbers. Missing map coverage is NULL, not zero, because absence on the map is not absence on the ground.
how: Collect features within a few decay lengths, compute distances, weight and sum. L and the weights are hypotheses to be fitted on labelled sites.

origin: Log-ratios are the standard way to compare two non-negative quantities symmetrically (compositional data analysis, Aitchison 1986): doubling one or halving the other moves the score by the same amount.
why: Classifiers work best with features that are symmetric and bounded in practice. A single log-ratio is easy to explain on the Sources page and robust to the overall density of mapped features.
how: Add one to each exposure and take the log of their ratio. If both are unknown the result is NULL.
example: Illustrative: IE 6.5, AE 2.5 → L = ln(7.5 / 3.5) = 0.762, industrial context. IE 5, AE 3 → ln(6/4) = 0.405.

formulas.name: Night fraction
formulas.status_text: Computed per site from detections; the exposure-adjusted form uses clear-sky day and night looks
formulas.lead: Factories, kilns and flares burn around the clock. Farmers burn residue in the afternoon. The share of a site's detections that come from night passes separates the two, once it is adjusted for how many day and night looks the satellite had.
equations: \nu_g = \frac{N^{\mathrm{N}}_g / E^{\mathrm{N}}_g}{N^{\mathrm{D}}_g / E^{\mathrm{D}}_g + N^{\mathrm{N}}_g / E^{\mathrm{N}}_g},\qquad \nu_g = \text{NULL if } N^{\mathrm{D}}_g + N^{\mathrm{N}}_g < 10
formulas.reads: The night fraction is the night detection rate per look divided by the sum of the day and night rates per look; with fewer than ten detections it is unknown.

symbols.meaning: Day and night detections at the site
Valid day and night observations
Night fraction

origin: Diurnal behaviour is a classic discriminator of fire type; studies of gas flares and industrial heat sources use night-time VIIRS detections because industry is hot at night while vegetation fires mostly are not.
why: Night fraction is one of the strongest pieces of evidence on the Sources page, and it guards the calendar: a site with a high night share is unlikely to be crop residue.
how: Count day and night detections at the site (a cluster or ~400 m site), divide each by its number of valid looks, and form the share. When looks are not yet loaded, the raw share is shown, which is close to the adjusted value for VIIRS because each platform makes one day and one night pass per day.
example: S-NPP sites with at least 10 detections in Punjab + Haryana (14,218 sites): the 45 sites FIRMS marks as static sources have a median night share of 0.86; farm-fire sites have a median of 0.00 (mean 0.011). Across all S-NPP detections only 2.6% are at night.

formulas.name: Diurnal fraction seen by overpasses
formulas.status_text: Running on the Blind Spot page as a scenario tool with the observed overpass windows
formulas.lead: Polar satellites look at each place only at fixed times. If farmers burn later in the afternoon, the fires happen between looks. This formula asks: if burning follows a daily curve, what share of it falls inside the moments the satellites are looking?
formulas.reads: The share seen is the integral of the daily burning curve over the union of all overpass windows, so overlapping windows are counted once.

symbols.meaning: Observed overpass time of platform o (local solar time)
Half-width of each window
Daily burning density (integrates to 1)
Union of windows: overlaps merged

origin: Diurnal sampling bias of polar orbiters is well documented (Giglio, 2007); geostationary sensors observe every 10–15 minutes and show the full daily cycle. The union is the correct way to combine windows: Aqua, S-NPP and NOAA-20 often look within minutes of each other and must not be counted three times.
why: Reports from Punjab in 2024–2025 describe burning shifting to late afternoon, after the satellite passes. If that is happening, falling detections could partly be a timing artefact. The Blind Spot page lets users move the burning peak and see how much the satellites would see. The result is a scenario, not a measured share of fires.
how: Take observed overpass times per platform from the data (median local solar time of daytime detections), build windows ±w, merge overlaps, and integrate a burning curve g over the merged windows. g is a scenario (here a normal curve) unless fitted to hourly geostationary data.
example: Observed 2024 windows over Punjab + Haryana (median daytime LMST): Terra 9:52, S-NPP 13:07, NOAA-20 13:07, Aqua 14:22. With w = 15 min and burning peaking at 13:00 (σ = 1.5 h), $f_{\mathrm{seen}}$ = 23.7%; adding the windows without merging would wrongly give 36.7%. If the peak moves to 16:18, the share seen drops to 7.3%.

formulas.name: Burned-area to detection ratio B
formulas.status_text: Defined; waits for MCD64A1 burned area from Earth Engine
formulas.lead: Burn scars stay visible for weeks; active-fire detections last minutes. If burned area per detection rises well above its usual level, detections may be missing burning. B is that warning flag: a disagreement indicator, never a multiplier.
equations: B = \text{PENDING while BA is lagged},\qquad B = \text{NULL if } C_{r,y} = 0
formulas.reads: B compares this year's burned area per detected cell-day with its median over reference years; it is pending while burned area is not yet published and unknown when no cell-days were detected.

symbols.meaning: Burned area (MCD64A1) in region r, season of year y
Detected fire cell-days
Reference years (at least 3)
Blind-spot ratio; ≥ 1.5 raises a 'check' flag

origin: Comparing burned-area and active-fire products is a standard consistency check (Giglio et al., 2018). The ratio of the two, normalised to a reference period, is a simple way to see when they diverge.
why: If farmers shift burning to times or conditions satellites cannot see (F45), detections fall faster than burning. Burned area, which does not depend on catching the fire alive, would then stay high. B makes that disagreement visible on the Blind Spot page and the Brief, without pretending to correct the counts.
how: For each season, divide burned area by detected cell-days, divide by the median of that ratio in reference years, and flag B ≥ 1.5. Burned area is published with a lag, so recent seasons are PENDING.
example: Illustrative: reference median 1.2 km² per cell-day; in a test year 2.9 km² per cell-day: B = 2.9 / 1.2 = 2.4 → 'check' flag. This would not mean real burning is 2.4× the detections; it means the two products disagree and the detections deserve scrutiny.
